about: The one list of Will Cook's websites, films, repositories and how they connect. The home page at wcook04.github.io, its catalogue.json graph and its llms.txt are built from it and from glossary.json. The build also writes family.json, the same list in the older v2 shape; each website keeps a copy of family.json for its own header, footer and video slots. Edit this file, then follow README.md, 'Add a released film'.

owner.name: Will Cook
owner.lede: I do mathematics research and build software with AI agents. I also build ways to inspect what the agents produce.
invitation: I’m looking for a job, internship, fellowship or funding, and I’m open to working with other people on their problems. If there’s a problem you think I should work on, please email me.
If something on these pages is unclear or wrong, please tell me. If your feedback leads to a change, I’d be happy to credit you, with your permission.
owner.orient: That means Lean proofs of AI-written mathematics, websites that display a paper beside its Lean code, and tools for running several coding agents in one repository. The introduction video explains how the projects fit together.
owner.availability: I’m looking for a job, internship, fellowship or research collaboration.

hero.headline: What would you like to understand?
hero.summary: Maths and code, made easier to follow.

presentation.projects_lede: Several projects use Lean, a proof assistant: software that accepts a proof only after verifying every step.

projects.name: Maths Map
projects.purpose: AI-assisted research on eight Erdős problems, with papers, records of failed approaches and Lean 4 proofs of partial results.
projects.status: Each problem page states whether the original question is still open and which statements the Lean proofs cover.
projects.capture_caption: Maths Map, open at Erdős problem #68.
projects.credit: Seven original questions remain open. The #1041 formal-statement counterexample is due to ani. The papers are not peer reviewed.
projects.label: Maths Map
projects.subject: Eight Erdős problems
projects.tagline: AI-assisted research on eight Erdős problems.
projects.summary: Find a theorem, read its research record or shorter paper, and open its available Lean or Comparator record. The map includes partial results and open questions.
projects.line: Browse results on eight Erdős problems, with paper links and available Lean checks.
projects.plain: Find the results and papers behind eight Erdős problems.

projects.name: SK Reader
projects.purpose: Three explanations of OpenAI’s full-support theorem for the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glass, linked to Lean declarations and an argument map.
projects.status: The site lists each Lean build and the statements it covers. Comparator gave no verdict on either theorem.
projects.capture_caption: The short paper at Theorem 1, beside the graph of its argument.
projects.credit: The theorem and Lean proof are OpenAI’s. I made the explanations and links with AI; no mathematician has reviewed them.
projects.label: SK Reader
projects.subject: Sherrington–Kirkpatrick spin glasses
projects.tagline: Papers and an argument map for OpenAI’s Sherrington–Kirkpatrick result.
projects.summary: Move between three AI-written papers, an authored argument map and linked passages of OpenAI’s Lean proof. The map explains the argument; it is distinct from a graph extracted from Lean declarations.
projects.line: Read explanations of OpenAI’s Sherrington–Kirkpatrick theorem beside its Lean proof.
projects.plain: Read a spin-glass result beside its computer-checked proof.

projects.name: General Reader
projects.purpose: Read Contextual Embeddings (PLDI 2026) beside its authors’ Lean proof, with statement-to-code links and a graph of proof dependencies.
projects.capture_caption: Contextual Embeddings beside the dependency graph and linked lines of its authors’ Lean proof.
projects.credit: Paper and proof by Frohlich, Foster, Kavvos and Wang. I made the reader and links with AI; the authors have not reviewed the links.
projects.label: General Reader
projects.subject: Papers beside Lean proofs
projects.tagline: A reusable reader for papers beside public Lean proofs.
projects.summary: The current example is Contextual Embeddings, a PLDI 2026 paper. Read its text beside the authors’ Lean proof, inspect declaration dependencies, and see the axioms used.
projects.line: Click a sentence in a paper to open the linked lines of its Lean proof.
projects.plain: Follow a paper’s sentences into the proof they describe.

projects.name: Quartic Reader
projects.purpose: Lean 4 formalisation of OpenAI’s nearly quartic randomized–quantum query-complexity separation, with mathematical expositions and a paragraph-linked proof reader.
projects.status: Comparator accepted each proof bundle in local runs on my computer and rejected five deliberately wrong solutions. The Forrelation lower bound, which the preprint imports, is proved here by a shorter route in a weaker form.
projects.capture_caption: The exposition beside the Lean dependency graph, following the paragraph being read.
projects.credit: Original theorem by OpenAI; formalisation and explanations made with AI. No human has reviewed whether the Lean statements match the paper.
projects.label: Quartic Reader
projects.subject: Randomized versus quantum query complexity
projects.tagline: The nearly quartic randomized–quantum query separation, explained beside Lean.
projects.summary: Follow the paper into linked Lean declarations, compare the formal statements with the prose, and explore their dependencies. The result concerns input queries; it is not a claim about full running time.
projects.line: Read OpenAI’s nearly quartic query separation beside its Lean 4 proof.
projects.plain: See how much quantum computation can reduce input queries.

projects.name: Plectis Atlas
projects.purpose: An index of OpenAI’s mathematics manuscripts, Lean statement files and published assessments, grouped into 372 paper families.
projects.status: I drafted the matches between each Lean statement and its paper with AI; no person has reviewed them.
projects.capture_caption: The Atlas map: each circle is a subject and each dot a family of papers.
projects.credit: Reports credited to MathVet, Carlos Toledo’s cert-machine and Neal McBurnett. I assembled the index and statement links with AI.
projects.label: Atlas
projects.subject: Outside reports on OpenAI’s maths
projects.tagline: OpenAI’s maths papers, with outside assessments alongside.
projects.summary: The supplied snapshot groups 719 papers into 372 families. The reader brings together source papers and attributed outside reports, including MathVet and cert-machine, so their statements and coverage labels can be compared.
projects.line: Browse OpenAI’s maths papers and compare the outside reports collected beside them.
projects.plain: Compare outside reports on the same maths paper.

projects.name: Practical Formal Verification
projects.purpose: Dafny proofs for 16 selected computations in an 88-component research-workflow prototype, with generated Python and proof-coverage maps.
projects.capture_caption: The system map: the 88 components in their seven families.
projects.credit: The proofs cover those computations, not the complete system.
projects.label: Formal verification
projects.subject: Dafny proofs in a Python toolkit
projects.tagline: A map of software components and the checks behind them.
projects.summary: Open the evidence rings to find calculation proofs, tests and design rules. The 16 calculations comprise 12 component-specific calculations and four shared ones; a proof of a calculation does not cover every claim about its component.
projects.line: Explore an 88-component Python toolkit with Dafny proofs for 16 calculations.
projects.plain: See which calculations have mathematical proofs.

projects.name: Zenith
projects.purpose: Experiments on whether records of earlier mistakes help language models test and repair code. The held-out testing study reports a mean per-problem fault-class detection score of 77.0%, compared with 69.2%.
projects.status: The held-out study used DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The earlier website and PDF describe separate studies, including program repairs rising from 259 to 365 of 576 tasks.
projects.capture_caption: The opening of the Zenith paper.
projects.credit: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on 58 held-out HumanEval problems; roughly half the gain came from timeouts. The supplied checkpoint links to the unmerged study revision.
projects.label: Zenith
projects.subject: AI-generated tests
projects.tagline: Testing whether missed-bug records help an AI generate better tests.
projects.summary: Compare prompts containing records of missed bugs with prompts containing generated rules. In this study the records improved the average per-problem score; roughly half the gain came from timeouts.
projects.line: Showing missed bugs raised DeepSeek V4.1 Flash’s average score from 69% to 77% on 58 held-out problems.
projects.plain: Can showing missed bugs improve the next set of tests?

projects.name: Code Ontology Bridge
projects.purpose: Exports Python code structure to DuckDB, with semantic descriptions and recursive SQL views for NVIDIA Auto Ontology’s text-to-SQL agent.
projects.status: AI models wrote the questions and answer keys; 21 answer keys were corrected after the runs. Every question, answer and failed run is published.
projects.capture_caption: Calls followed backwards from a function, with a callback reference shown dashed.
projects.credit: Independent of NVIDIA. The 12-question comparison measured Auto Ontology plus the code database against DeepSeek alone. The separate no-clear-improvement result concerns adding descriptions within Auto Ontology, not the gain from the whole setup.
projects.label: Code Ontology Bridge
projects.subject: NVIDIA Auto Ontology for code
projects.tagline: A code database and semantic models for NVIDIA Auto Ontology.
projects.summary: Static analysis turns Python code into a DuckDB database of functions and call relations. The bridge supplies that structure to NVIDIA Auto Ontology, with rerunnable SQL queries and a code-question study.
projects.line: Query Python functions and calls through DuckDB and NVIDIA Auto Ontology.
projects.plain: Ask questions about functions and the code that calls them.

projects.name: Agent Trace
projects.purpose: Local Codex and Claude Code session viewer with tool traces, selective context export and optional MCP access.
projects.credit: Technical preview; browser app or native Mac window.
projects.label: Agent Trace
projects.subject: Claude Code and Codex sessions
projects.tagline: Saved coding sessions you can inspect and copy.
projects.summary: Select a session, inspect its recorded commands and output, and copy a chosen level of detail into another chat. An optional MCP interface exposes those saved records to supported clients.
projects.line: Inspect saved Claude Code and Codex sessions, with commands beside their output.
projects.plain: See the commands and results saved by a coding assistant.

projects.name: Narration IR
projects.purpose: A skill for writing an intermediate representation between narration and animation: sentence meanings, source quotations, what each picture should explain, and cues tied to spoken words.
projects.label: Narration IR
projects.subject: Narration into picture plans
projects.tagline: A readable plan between the script and the animation.
projects.summary: For each sentence, specify what the audience needs to understand and attach picture events to spoken words. Source quotations and word identifiers make the plan easier to inspect before animation code is written.
projects.line: Turn narration into a plan of sentence meanings, source quotations and word-timed picture changes.
projects.plain: Plan what each picture should explain.

projects.name: Safety Core
projects.purpose: Generates AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and command-enforcement hooks from one rulebook, distinguishing written instructions from rules enforced by hooks.
projects.credit: Tested in one small Claude Haiku study; the enforcement rule was written after observing the failure.
projects.label: Safety Core
projects.subject: Rules and command checks
projects.tagline: Written rules and executable checks for coding agents.
projects.summary: Explore the rulebook and tests, then compare written instructions with checks run before commands. The videos show specific cases involving made-up settings, false success reports and exposed keys.
projects.line: Combine an editable rulebook with Claude Code hooks that check selected commands.
projects.plain: Set rules for coding agents and check commands before they run.

projects.name: One Checkout
projects.purpose: Commits a reviewed Git patch while preserving another agent’s unfinished staged and working-tree edits, including changes in the same files.
projects.label: One Checkout
projects.subject: Several agents in one checkout
projects.tagline: Selected commits from a shared checkout.
projects.summary: Build a commit from the last committed version and one selected patch. Other unfinished edits stay in the working tree, including edits to the same file.
projects.line: Commit one agent’s Git patch while unfinished edits remain in the same working tree.
projects.plain: Save one finished fix while another agent is still editing.

projects.name: CodeMap
projects.purpose: A code browser with docstring descriptions and function-call links, available to both the human reader and coding agents.
projects.status: Not released; the video shows it in use.
projects.credit: Private software; the video shows it in use.
projects.label: CodeMap
projects.subject: Maps of a codebase
projects.tagline: A map drawn from the descriptions kept with the code.
projects.summary: Move from the repository overview to individual files, their saved docstrings and call links. Coding agents can retrieve those same descriptions as text.
projects.line: Explore a codebase through saved file descriptions and links between functions.
projects.plain: Find a file, read its description and follow its calls.

projects.name: The funnel
projects.label: The funnel
projects.subject: A proof into papers and video
projects.purpose: Instructions for turning a Lean proof into a research record, specialist paper, exposition and video, with linked reader websites.
projects.tagline: Instructions for explaining the same result at different levels.
projects.summary: The worked example is a case of Erdős #257. Follow its formal proof through the four outputs, then see related reader websites for OpenAI’s spin-glass and quantum query results.
projects.line: Turn a Lean proof into a research record, specialist paper, exposition and video.
projects.plain: Follow one proof into explanations for different readers.
